title: Natural linear comparison of equivariant coequalizer presentations
statement:
Let $\mathcal D$ be a monoidal category [def-sfb-monoidal-category], $A$ a monoid object [sk-def-sfb-ring-object], and $J$ a category. Write $U:\operatorname{Mod}_A(\mathcal D)\to\mathcal D$ for the forgetful functor [sk-def-sfb-module-objects]. Let $H:J\to\mathcal D$ and $B,P,Q:J\to\operatorname{Mod}_A(\mathcal D)$ be functors, and let $a,b:H\Rightarrow U\circ B$ be natural transformations. Suppose $q:U\circ B\Rightarrow U\circ P$ and $r:U\circ B\Rightarrow U\circ Q$ are natural transformations such that, for every $j\in J$:
(1) $q_j:B_j\to P_j$ and $r_j:B_j\to Q_j$ are coequalizers of $a_j,b_j$ in $\mathcal D$; explicitly $q_ja_j=q_jb_j$, and every $h:B_j\to T$ equalizing $a_j,b_j$ factors uniquely as $h=kq_j$, and likewise for $r_j$;
(2) writing $\beta_j,\delta^P_j,\delta^Q_j$ for the $A$-actions, one has
\[
q_j\circ\beta_j=\delta^P_j\circ(1_A\otimes q_j),\qquad r_j\circ\beta_j=\delta^Q_j\circ(1_A\otimes r_j);
\]
(3) $A\otimes-$ preserves these coequalizers, meaning $1_A\otimes q_j$ and $1_A\otimes r_j$ are coequalizers of $1_A\otimes a_j,1_A\otimes b_j$.
There is a unique natural isomorphism $c:Q\xrightarrow{\sim}P$ of $A$-module-valued functors whose underlying components satisfy $c_j\circ r_j=q_j$. Its inverse $d:P\xrightarrow{\sim}Q$ satisfies $d_j\circ q_j=r_j$. In particular,
\[
c_j\delta^Q_j=\delta^P_j(1_A\otimes c_j),\quad d_j\delta^P_j=\delta^Q_j(1_A\otimes d_j),\quad P(u)c_j=c_kQ(u)
\]
for every $u:j\to k$ in $J$, and $d_jc_j=1_{Q_j}$, $c_jd_j=1_{P_j}$. No colimit indexed by $J$, smallness of $J$, or module structure on $H_j$ is required.

proof.text: We will use only the uniqueness in the coequalizer property explicitly assumed in (1) and (3). If $e:Y\to Z$ is any one of these coequalizers, of a pair $s,t:X\rightrightarrows Y$, and $f,g:Z\to T$ satisfy $fe=ge$, put $h=fe=ge$. Then $hs=fes=fet=ht$, and both $f$ and $g$ are factorizations of $h$ through $e$. Uniqueness gives $f=g$. This argument applies to $q_j,r_j,1_A\otimes q_j,1_A\otimes r_j$ with their respective parallel pairs.

source.place: Tag 002A, definition-coequalizers: direct universal-property argument; equivariance and naturality refinement written by Q26

proof.text: Fix $j$. Since $q_ja_j=q_jb_j$, the coequalizer property of $r_j$ in (1), with $T=P_j$ and $h=q_j$, gives a unique $c_j:Q_j\to P_j$ such that $c_jr_j=q_j$. Since $r_ja_j=r_jb_j$, the coequalizer property of $q_j$, with $T=Q_j$ and $h=r_j$, gives a unique $d_j:P_j\to Q_j$ such that $d_jq_j=r_j$. These are morphisms in $\mathcal D$ at this point; no action on $H_j$ was used.

source.place: Tag 002A, definition-coequalizers: direct universal-property argument; equivariance and naturality refinement written by Q26

proof.text: The two composites satisfy $(d_jc_j)r_j=d_jq_j=r_j=1_{Q_j}r_j$ and $(c_jd_j)q_j=c_jr_j=q_j=1_{P_j}q_j$. Applying the uniqueness argument in step 1 to $r_j$ and $q_j$, respectively, proves $d_jc_j=1_{Q_j}$ and $c_jd_j=1_{P_j}$. Thus the underlying morphisms are inverse isomorphisms.

source.place: Tag 002A, definition-coequalizers: direct universal-property argument; equivariance and naturality refinement written by Q26

proof.text:
To check the action equation for $c_j$, compute the following equality of morphisms $A\otimes B_j\to P_j$ using (2) and step 2:
\[
(c_j\delta^Q_j)(1_A\otimes r_j)=c_jr_j\beta_j=q_j\beta_j=\delta^P_j(1_A\otimes q_j)=\delta^P_j(1_A\otimes c_j)(1_A\otimes r_j).
\]
The last equality uses preservation of composition by the tensor bifunctor of [def-sfb-monoidal-category]. By (3), $1_A\otimes r_j$ is a coequalizer, so step 1 gives $c_j\delta^Q_j=\delta^P_j(1_A\otimes c_j)$. By clause 2 of [sk-def-sfb-module-objects], this makes $c_j$ an $A$-module morphism.

source.place: Tag 002A, definition-coequalizers: direct universal-property argument; equivariance and naturality refinement written by Q26

proof.text:
For the inverse, (2) and step 2 give an equality of morphisms $A\otimes B_j\to Q_j$:
\[
(d_j\delta^P_j)(1_A\otimes q_j)=d_jq_j\beta_j=r_j\beta_j=\delta^Q_j(1_A\otimes r_j)=\delta^Q_j(1_A\otimes d_j)(1_A\otimes q_j).
\]
Here the final equality again uses the tensor bifunctor law of [def-sfb-monoidal-category]. Hypothesis (3) and step 1 cancel $1_A\otimes q_j$, giving $d_j\delta^P_j=\delta^Q_j(1_A\otimes d_j)$. Clause 2 of [sk-def-sfb-module-objects] therefore makes $d_j$ an $A$-module morphism.

source.place: Tag 002A, definition-coequalizers: direct universal-property argument; equivariance and naturality refinement written by Q26

proof.text:
For any $u:j\to k$, naturality of the assumed transformations $q$ and $r$ and the defining equations of step 2 give
\[
(P(u)c_j)r_j=P(u)q_j=q_kB(u)=c_kr_kB(u)=(c_kQ(u))r_j.
\]
All these composites have source $B_j$ and target $P_k$. Step 1 applied to $r_j$ proves $P(u)c_j=c_kQ(u)$. Since module morphisms are the underlying morphisms satisfying the action equation, with the same composition, as in [sk-def-sfb-module-objects], this equality is the naturality equation in the module category as well.

source.place: Tag 002A, definition-coequalizers: direct universal-property argument; equivariance and naturality refinement written by Q26

proof.text:
The inverse family is natural too: for $u:j\to k$,
\[
(Q(u)d_j)q_j=Q(u)r_j=r_kB(u)=d_kq_kB(u)=(d_kP(u))q_j.
\]
Step 1 applied to $q_j$ proves $Q(u)d_j=d_kP(u)$. As in [sk-def-sfb-module-objects], the equality of these underlying module morphisms is precisely their equality in the module category.

source.place: Tag 002A, definition-coequalizers: direct universal-property argument; equivariance and naturality refinement written by Q26

proof.text: Steps 4 and 6 assemble the components into a natural transformation $c:Q\Rightarrow P$ of module-valued functors; steps 5 and 7 assemble $d:P\Rightarrow Q$. Their composites are the identity transformations because their components are identities by step 3 and module morphisms have the underlying composition of [sk-def-sfb-module-objects]. Thus they form the required natural isomorphism. If $c'$ is any other such isomorphism, then $c'_jr_j=q_j=c_jr_j$ for every $j$, so step 1 gives $c'_j=c_j$; hence $c'=c$. The inverse equations give the asserted normalization of $d$. The construction and every check were at an object or an arrow of $J$: no colimit over $J$, smallness assumption on $J$, or module structure on $H_j$ was introduced.
